name: Hana Schmidt

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group that doesn't work for AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me both what you'd say in public and what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work for Mr Brandt on his hill farm, about sixty suckler cows, that's beef cows that raise their own calves, and a few fields of hay and oats. He's seventy-one and his wife passed, so it's him, me, and a contractor at harvest. I feed, check the cows, fix fences, and in summer I turn hay till my arms shake. I started four years ago when Mila went to school, before that I cleaned holiday cottages.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What's the part you're still learning?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Nearly all of it, if I'm honest. I can't back a trailer straight yet, and calving still frightens me, Mr Brandt does the hard ones. I write everything in a notebook, which cow, which field, what the vet said, because I don't trust the phone and I don't use any of those AI things. Jonas works at the sawmill, we've got Lukas and Mila, a mortgage, and less than a month put by.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it was a fuss about nothing much, same as most things on the news. I'd probably not say it online, I don't really go online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means my week looks like my week. Fine by me. I'd rather be broke and know what Tuesday looks like than be broke and not know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going at Brandt's and keep my notebook. Maybe ask him to teach me the calving properly this spring. Same as I'd do anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Tired, but that's the hay, not the computers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does anything about Mr Brandt's farm worry you, even in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: His age. He's got a nephew in the city who'd sell it the minute he could. That's my real worry, not robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if he sold?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Look for work at the next farm, but there's only two others in the valley that hire, and they've got their people. Probably go back to cleaning. It pays about the same, it's just harder on the soul.

S0.say: She'd say AI was a fuss about nothing, like most things on the news. She rarely goes online, so she'd mostly say it in person.
S0.think: Privately she's glad her week would stay predictable. Even if money is tight, she prefers knowing what each day holds.
S0.do: Keeps working on the hill farm and keeps her paper notebook. Asks her employer to teach her calving properly this spring.
S0.feel: Calm, tired from the work rather than worried.
S0.quote: I'd rather be broke and know what Tuesday looks like than be broke and not know.
S0.fieldNote: Her real worry is her elderly employer's nephew selling the farm, not technology. Cleaning is her known fallback, which she describes as harder on the soul. She values predictability above almost everything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say well, everyone's going to have to cope, aren't they. I wouldn't make speeches about it, I'd just say it's change and we'll see.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think this is when the nephew sells. A big outfit with machines would buy the land, run it with half the people, and I'm not even half a person to them, I'm the one who can't back a trailer. That'd be me gone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop the kids' swimming lessons and put that money aside, forty a month. I'd ask Mr Brandt straight what his plans are, which I've never dared. And I'd wait a bit before doing anything else, because I don't know what else there is to do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Knotted up. I'd be sharp with the kids and then sorry about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've never dared ask Mr Brandt. What's stopped you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels like asking someone when they're going to die. He's been good to me. You don't walk into a man's kitchen and ask him who gets the cows after the funeral.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you consider learning to use any of the new tools, to make yourself harder to replace?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd think about it and probably not do it. Lukas tried to put an app on my phone for the cattle records and I deleted it the next day. I'm not proud of it, I just freeze in front of those things.

S1.say: She'd say everyone will have to cope with the change, without making speeches. Her public line is a shrug: it's change and we'll see.
S1.think: Privately she thinks this is when her employer's nephew sells to a big farm that runs with fewer people. As the least skilled worker, she expects to be the one who goes.
S1.do: Stops the children's swimming lessons to set aside forty a month. Finally asks her employer about his plans, then waits before doing anything else.
S1.feel: Knotted up, short-tempered with the kids and then sorry.
S1.quote: You don't walk into a man's kitchen and ask him who gets the cows after the funeral.
S1.fieldNote: Mild public words hide a specific private fear tied to one elderly man's will. She knows learning tools might help but admits she freezes and deleted the app her son installed. Her centre outlook shows as acceptance without blame.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say somebody in charge had better have a plan, because I don't. I wouldn't blame one side, it's just come too quick for anyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think both of us lose our jobs, me and Jonas. The sawmill's already half machines. Two years and there's no farm job, no mill job, and the cleaning will be robots too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to the council office the first week and ask what help there is, which I've never done in my life. I'd cut everything, the car insurance down to the minimum, no Christmas presents but small ones. I'd ask my mother if we could move in with her if we lose the house, she's got the spare rooms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like the floor's gone. I can't think past it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything the two years would let you do, even a little?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really. Two years is two hay seasons. I'm still learning to back a trailer, and they're telling me the trailer will drive itself before I've got it straight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said cleaning would go too. What would be left?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know, and that's the honest answer. Looking after my mum, maybe, she's getting on. I'd do whatever there was, I'm not fussy, there just wouldn't be anything.

S2.say: She'd say someone in charge had better have a plan, because she doesn't. She wouldn't blame either side, just the speed of it.
S2.think: Privately she expects both she and her partner to lose work, since the sawmill is already partly automated. Even her fallback, cleaning, would be done by robots.
S2.do: Goes to the council office in the first week to ask about help for the first time in her life. Cuts car insurance to the minimum and Christmas to small presents, and asks her mother about moving in if they lose the house.
S2.feel: As if the floor has gone, unable to think past it.
S2.quote: I'm still learning to back a trailer, and they're telling me the trailer will drive itself before I've got it straight.
S2.fieldNote: Every option she knows disappears at once: farm, sawmill and cleaning. Her low skill and resistance to technology leave her no foothold, and she says so plainly. She'd turn to family and the council despite never having done so.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is something, let's use it sensibly. I'd want the council or somebody to tell us plainly what's coming to our valley.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years is still too fast for someone like me. It's enough to see it coming but not enough to become somebody else. Maybe it's enough for Mr Brandt to see it out and leave me the job until it ends.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put away whatever I could, starting at twenty a week, and stop the car loan going any longer. I'd ask about a care assistant course at the college, because people will want a person caring for their old mum. I'd keep working for Brandt every day I could.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, but more the slow kind. Like waiting for test results.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: A care course is a big change. Would you actually do it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd look at the leaflet for a month and then probably do it, because Jonas would push me. I looked after my gran at the end. Cows and old people aren't so different: they both want you there on time, and both know when you're faking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would five years do for Lukas and Mila?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Lukas would be eighteen, so he'd be out of school, and that's a weight off. Mila would be thirteen, still needing everything. It's Mila I'd be counting on my fingers about.

S3.say: She'd say five years is something to use sensibly. She'd want the council or someone to explain plainly what's coming to her valley.
S3.think: Privately she thinks five years is still too fast for her to become someone new. She hopes her employer keeps her on until the end.
S3.do: Saves twenty a week and avoids extending the car loan. Looks into a care assistant course at the college, pushed by her partner, while working every day she can on the farm.
S3.feel: Scared in a slow way, like waiting for test results.
S3.quote: Cows and old people aren't so different: they both want you there on time, and both know when you're faking.
S3.fieldNote: The extra time doesn't make her adaptable, but it lets her consider care work, linked to her experience nursing her grandmother. She leans on her partner to push her into change. Her children's ages frame what the time is worth.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is fair warning, so there's no excuse for anyone being caught out. I'd tell the women at the school gate the same.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, ten years I can live with. I'd be fifty-three, the kids grown, and by then I'd have found something or Mr Brandt would have retired and I'd have moved on anyway. It's the same ending, but I'd be walking into it, not falling.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait a year or two to see what everyone else does, honestly. Then I'd take the care course and keep a bit saved each month. I'd keep my notebook and my cows till they tell me to stop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but I'd sleep. I couldn't sleep in the fast one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd wait a year or two. Isn't that time you could use?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably. Jonas would say so. But I've been wrong rushing into things before, I left a good cleaning job for a worse one because of the money. I'd rather watch the first lot try and copy whoever doesn't fall in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you watch?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The young lad at the Kemps' farm who's always on his phone, and my neighbour Ruth, who did the care course already. If she's still in work in five years, that's my answer.

S4.say: She'd say ten years is fair warning and no one should be caught out. She'd say the same to other parents at the school gate.
S4.think: Privately she can live with ten years, ending at fifty-three with grown children. It's the same ending, but she'd walk into it rather than fall.
S4.do: Waits a year or two to see how others fare before acting. Then takes the care course, saves a little each month and keeps working with the cattle until told to stop.
S4.feel: Worried, but able to sleep, unlike in the fast picture.
S4.quote: I'd rather watch the first lot try and copy whoever doesn't fall in.
S4.fieldNote: Ten years matches her habit of watching others first; she names specific people she'd copy. She admits waiting may waste time. The difference between falling and walking into the change captures what time means to her.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because there's nothing to grab on to. What would help is someone telling us straight what's coming to our valley, and help with the mortgage so we don't lose the roof while we sort ourselves out. Not a website, a person.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask about people like me who aren't good with computers. Everybody assumes we'll just learn. Some of us were never the quick ones, and nobody builds the future with the slow ones in mind.

headlineQuote: Some of us were never the quick ones, and nobody builds the future with the slow ones in mind.
portrait: Hana Schmidt is a 43-year-old junior hand on an elderly widower's hill farm with sixty beef cows and some hay and oats. She started four years ago after cleaning holiday cottages, keeps all her records in a paper notebook and never uses AI tools. She lives with her partner Jonas, a sawmill worker, and their two children, with a mortgage and less than a month saved. Calm in the plateau, she is anxious under steady change because her employer's nephew might sell, panicked by two-year AGI, and steadier only with ten years, when she'd watch others and then train in care work. She asks for plain information and help with the mortgage.
biggestWorry: AGI within two years, because her farm job, her partner's sawmill job and her fallback cleaning work would all go at once.
whatWouldHelp: A real person telling her valley plainly what's coming, and help with the mortgage while the family finds new work.
